[0] everyday_reading (E): The everyday 'graph of a function' is an exact, smooth curve. A program can only evaluate the function at finitely many sampled points and join them with straight segments.
[1] misconception (M) -> PlotIsExactCurve: wrong rule: The drawn plot is the exact curve. Right rule: The plot is a piecewise linear approximation through the sampled points. With too few samples it can miss major fluctuations.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> PlotIsExactCurve: Points to LT (fill x[], fill y[], set the scales, then draw segment i from point i-1 to point i). An uneven trace pairs x[i] with y[i-1], or draws before setting the scale. (here mixing in: "The drawn plot is the exact curve")

[0] names_the_element (N): Function plotting is a sampling technique: evaluate f at evenly spaced x-values, store the values in arrays, set the scales, and connect consecutive points with lines.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Sample the function by choosing x-values and evaluating f at each one. Connecting successive points with lines gives a piecewise linear approximation.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): 1) x[i] = Math.PI * i / N for i = 0..N. 2) y[i] = f(x[i]). 3) setXscale and setYscale. 4) For i = 1..N, line(x[i-1], y[i-1], x[i], y[i]).
[1] output_prediction (OP): The plot is N line segments through N+1 sample points. With N = 20 the curve is jagged and misses wiggles; with N = 200 it looks smooth.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One drawing iteration draws one segment between consecutive samples i-1 and i. It changes no array values.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): The arrays have N+1 elements (indices 0..N). The drawing loop starts at i = 1 so that x[i-1] stays in bounds; starting at 0 would access x[-1].
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): A sound wave is sampled at regular intervals in exactly the way a function is sampled for plotting. The same array can be drawn or played.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): The x-scale must match the sampled interval and the y-scale the function's range; otherwise the curve is clipped or squashed.
[3] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan: sample, then connect (a prototypical sampling computation). The arrays are containers of samples and i is a stepper.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> PlotIsExactCurve: Increasing N makes the curve smoother and keeps the end points, but costs time. Decreasing N keeps the sampled points but can lose features between them.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use sampled plotting to see the shape of a function or data series. For exact values, print them. For smooth curves with few points, the book later uses a different method (Section 2.4).
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Array indices must stay in 0..N. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: The drawing loop starts at i = 0 (so x[i-1] is x[-1]) or runs to i <= N+1: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The sample must be dense enough for the function. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: N is too small for a rapidly oscillating f, so the plot misses major fluctuations.
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The y-scale must cover the function's range. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: The default unit square, or a wrong y-range, cuts off the negative part of sin(4x) + sin(20x).
wrong: The drawn plot is the exact curve. | right: It is a piecewise linear approximation through the sampled points.
The sample points are kept in arrays and traversed.
Before plotting, the x-scale is set to the interval and the y-scale to the range of function values so the curve fits the canvas.
A sound wave is sampled at regular intervals exactly as a function is sampled for plotting, giving the array of samples that StdAudio plays.
A function is plotted by drawing its sampled points and lines with StdDraw.
